translation: Therefore he especially valued the principle of the lawfulness [закономерность] of the processes of nature, which contemporary science values much less. The new natural reality before which contemporary technics [техника] places man is not at all a product of evolution, but a product of the inventiveness and creative activity of man himself, not of an organic process but of an organizational process. With this is bound up the meaning of the whole technical epoch. The dominion of technics and the machine is above all a transition from organic life to organized life, from vegetative growth [растительность] to constructiveness. From the point of view of organic life, technics means disincarnation [развоплощение], a rupture in the organic bodies of history, a rupture of flesh and spirit [дух]. Technics discloses a new stage of reality, and this reality is the creation of man, the result of the breaking-through of spirit into nature and the implanting of reason into elemental [стихийные] processes. Technics destroys old bodies and creates new bodies, quite unlike organic bodies; it creates organized bodies. And here is the tragedy: the creation rises up against its creator and no longer obeys him. The mystery of the Fall is in the revolt of the creature against the Creator. It is repeated in the whole history of mankind as well. The Promethean spirit of man is not strong enough to master the technics it has created, to cope with the unfettered, unprecedented energies. We see this in all the processes of rationalization in the technical epoch, when man is replaced by the machine. Technics replaces the organic-irrational with the organized-rational. But it gives rise to new irrational consequences in social life. Thus the rationalization of industry gives rise to unemployment, the greatest calamity of our time. Man's labour is replaced by the machine; this is a positive conquest, which ought to have abolished the slavery and poverty of man. But the machine does not at all obey what man demands of it; it dictates its own laws. Man said to the machine: I need you to ease my life, to increase my strength; but the machine answered man: and I do not need you, I shall do everything without you, and you may perish. The Taylor system is the extreme form of the rationalization of labour, but it turns man into a perfected machine. The machine wants man to take on its image and likeness. But man is the image and likeness of God and cannot become the image and likeness of the machine without ceasing to exist. Here we come up against the limits of the transition from the organic-irrational to the organized-rational. Organization connected with technics presupposes an organizing subject, that is, an organism, and it cannot itself be turned into a machine. But organization has a tendency
notes: The opening 'he' refers to a figure named in preceding text not supplied. Passage breaks off mid-sentence ('имеет тенденцию').

relevance.reason: It frames reliance on the machine in theological terms close to idolatry (Q31): the creature's revolt against its creator repeats the Fall, and the machine demands that man take on its image and likeness in place of God's, which he cannot do without ceasing to exist.

translation: Technics [техника] has a cosmogonic significance; through it a new cosmos is created. Lafitte, in the recently published book “Réflexions sur la science des machines”, says that alongside inorganic and organic bodies there are also organized bodies: the kingdom of machines, a special kingdom. This is a new category of being. The machine is indeed neither an inorganic nor an organic body. The appearance of these new bodies is bound up with the distinction between the organic and the organized. It would be completely mistaken to assign the machine to the inorganic world on the grounds that elements of inorganic bodies, taken from mechanical-physical-chemical reality, are used for its organization. In inorganic nature machines do not exist; they exist only in the social world. These organized bodies appear not before man, as inorganic bodies do, but after man and through man. Man has succeeded in calling into life, in realizing, a new reality. This is an index of man's terrible power. It points to his creative and kingly vocation in the world. But it is also an index of his weakness, of his inclination to slavery. The machine has an enormous significance, not only sociological but cosmological as well, and it poses with extraordinary acuteness the problem of the destiny of man in society and in the cosmos. This is the problem of the relation of man to nature, of personality to society, of spirit [дух] to matter, of the irrational to the rational. It is striking that up to now no philosophy of technics and the machine has been created, although many books have been written on this subject. Much has already been prepared for the creation of such a philosophy, but the most important thing has not been done: the machine and technics have not been grasped as a spiritual problem, as the destiny of man. The machine is considered only from outside, only in social projection. But from within it is a theme of the philosophy of human existence (Existenzphilosophie). Can man exist only in the old cosmos, physical and organic, which appeared to be an eternal order, or can he exist also in a new, other, as yet unknown cosmos? Christianity, with which the destiny of man is bound up, is placed before a new world, and it has not yet made sense of its new position. On this depends also the construction of a philosophy of technics, for the question must be resolved in spiritual experience before it is resolved in philosophical cognition. So it always is, even if philosophical cognition does not notice it [ 4 ].
notes: Title of Jacques Lafitte's book (1932) appears without the accent ('Reflexions'); given with accent in the English. '[ 4 ]' is a footnote marker.

relevance.reason: It calls the machine a new category of being and a spiritual problem that Christianity has not yet thought through, but takes no position on whether reliance on machinery can become idolatry (Q31).

translation: What is the chief danger that the machine brings with it for man, a danger that has already fully revealed itself? I do not think that it is chiefly a danger for spirit [дух] and spiritual life. The machine and technics inflict terrible defeats on the soul-life [душевная жизнь] of man, and above all on emotional life, on human feelings. The element [стихия] of soul and emotion is dying out in contemporary civilization. So one can say that the old culture was dangerous for the human body; it left it in neglect, often pampered and weakened it. Machine technical civilization is dangerous above all for the soul [душа]. The heart can hardly bear the touch of cold metal; it cannot live in a metallic environment. Processes of the destruction of the heart, as the core of the soul, are characteristic of our epoch. In the greatest French writers of our epoch, e.g. Proust and Gide, one can no longer find the heart as an integral organ of man's soul-life. Everything has decomposed into an intellectual element and into sensual sensations. Keyserling is completely right when he speaks of the destruction of the emotional order in contemporary technical civilization and wants the restoration of this order [ 5 ]. Technics deals terrible blows to humanism, to the humanist world-view, to the humanist ideal of man and culture. The machine is by its nature anti-humanist. The technical understanding of science is completely opposed to the humanist understanding of science and comes into conflict with the humanist understanding of the fullness of humanity. This is all the same question of the relation to the soul. Technics is less dangerous for spirit, although at first glance this may be surprising. In reality one can say that we live in an epoch of technics and spirit, not in an epoch of soulfulness [душевность]. The religious meaning of contemporary technics lies precisely in this, that it places everything under the sign of the spiritual question, and therefore it can also lead to spiritualization [?: the text reads 'одухотворенно', 'in a spiritualized way']. It demands a straining of spirituality.

terms.english: soul-life (psychic-emotional life, as distinct from spirit)

notes: 'к одухотворенно' is ungrammatical and probably a truncation of 'к одухотворенности' (to spiritualization); flagged, not corrected. '[ 5 ]' is a footnote marker.

relevance.reason: It argues that the machine endangers the soul more than the spirit and that technics has a religious meaning because it forces the spiritual question, which bears on Q31 but argues against treating technics mainly as a spiritual threat and does not speak of idolatry.

translation: But he became the slave of the state, of nationality, of classes. Now he is entering a new period. He wants to master the irrational social forces. He creates an organized society and a developed technics [техника], makes man an instrument of the organization of life and of the final mastery of nature. But he becomes the slave of organized society and of technics, the slave of the machine into which society has been turned and into which man himself is imperceptibly being turned. But in ever new forms the problem is posed of the liberation of man, of the mastery by spirit [дух] of nature and society [?: of mastering the spirit of nature and society]. This problem can be solved only by a consciousness that will place man above nature and society, will place the human soul above all natural and social forces, which must submit to him. What liberated man must be accepted, and what enslaved him rejected. But this truth about man, about his dignity and his vocation, is laid down in Christianity, although perhaps it has been insufficiently disclosed in its history and often distorted. The path of the final liberation of man and of the final realization of his vocation is the path to the Kingdom of God, which is not only the kingdom of heaven but also the kingdom of a transfigured earth, of a transfigured cosmos. ↑ That the highest values are the least strong is well said by N. Hartmann in his “Ethik”. ↑ See e.g. Maritain's book “Art et scolastique”. ↑ An essay in the philosophy of technics is Friedrich Dessauer's book “Philosophie der Technik”. ↑ The interesting book by Cina Lombroso, “La rancon du machinisme”, is permeated by too great a faith in the possibility of a return to domestic types of civilization. ↑ See the interesting book by Setnitsky, “On the Final Ideal”. Setnitsky's book represents the Fedorovian tendency in the Soviet period. In it the traditionally religious elements of N. Fedorov's world-view have weakened.
notes: The opening 'he' refers to man in the preceding text (not supplied). The passage runs into the chapter's endnotes (marked ↑). 'Cina Lombroso' is presumably Gina Lombroso and 'La rancon' presumably 'La rançon'; left as printed. Setnitsky's title is 'О конечном идеале'.

relevance.reason: It holds that man has become the slave of the machine and that liberation lies only in the Christian truth about man and the path to the Kingdom of God, a religious answer relevant to Q31 that does not use the idea of idolatry.
